Listen to this article Share The Nigeria Economic Summit Group has called for the establishment of an industrialisation, competitiveness and regional integration council within the Presidency to coordinate government policies, address structural constraints and strengthen Nigeria’s manufacturing capacity as the country seeks to expand its presence in African markets. The proposed council would provide a central coordinating platform linking the Presidency, relevant government institutions and private-sector operators to accelerate industrial development, improve implementation of the country’s industrial policy and position Nigerian businesses to compete more effectively under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). The call followed discussions at a breakout session on building an integrated industrial ecosystem during the 32nd Nigeria Economic Summit in Abuja on Tuesday, where stakeholders identified persistent challenges in energy supply, transportation and logistics, access to finance, human capital development, local manufacturing and export competitiveness. Lumun Feese, co-facilitator of the NESG who moderated the session, said Nigeria needed a coordinated approach to industrialisation rather than addressing individual sectoral challenges in isolation. She said the country’s position on the African Development Bank’s Africa Industrialisation Index had fallen from eighth place in the previous edition to 14th in the latest ranking, although he noted that the methodology had changed and more countries had been included. According to her, Nigeria’s position was disappointing given its large population, natural resources and economic potential. “We are not maximising our potential and our large economy,” Feese said, stressing that the country needed to move beyond dependence on its domestic market and develop the competitiveness required to supply other African economies. She argued that the size of Nigeria’s domestic market had made some businesses comfortable with selling locally instead of investing in the capacity, quality standards and operational efficiency needed to compete internationally. Read also: Dangote Cement’s Nigeria business generates N1.6tn EBITDA as Pan-African earnings weaken AfCFTA, she said, offered Nigerian manufacturers access to a much larger market, but taking advantage of that opportunity would require lower production costs, improved infrastructure and stronger integration across the economy. “How do we go and compete in South Africa when our cost of production is so high? Power, logistics and so on and so forth,” she asked. Feese said Nigeria’s industrial policy was aligned with the African market but required stronger integration with other African Union frameworks designed to support regional value chains, technological upgrading and infrastructure development. She called for closer collaboration between government and the private sector, arguing that industrialisation would depend on bringing together systems that currently operate separately. She cited the need to integrate gas-fired power generation with renewable energy, as well as rail, road, maritime and air transportation, to improve the movement of goods and reduce costs for manufacturers. “Industrialisation is us bringing all these systems together to work together and not in isolation,” she said. The proposed council, she added, would provide a central institutional champion within the Presidency to coordinate these efforts and ensure that industrial development received sustained attention across successive administrations. Read also: Nigeria’s domestic economy will benefit from stronger links to its vast gas reserves Gerald Okunsebor, Special Assistant on Strategy to the Minister of State for Industry, said Nigeria needed to improve public awareness of its National Industrial Policy (NIP) and establish clearer mechanisms for implementation and private-sector participation. Presenting the findings of the third working group, Okunsebor said discussions revealed that several participants were unaware of the existence of the policy, highlighting what he described as inadequate government efforts to communicate its provisions to businesses and other stakeholders. He said the policy needed to be made more accessible, with a deliberate sensitisation strategy to ensure that relevant industries, investors and members of the public understood its objectives and could contribute to its implementation. Okunsebor said the government should establish an implementation framework containing clear timelines, defined responsibilities and accountability mechanisms to ensure that the policy translated into measurable industrial outcomes. He also advocated a central knowledge-management system that would preserve institutional experience and policy information beyond changes in government. Such a system, he said, would allow incoming administrations to build on existing work rather than repeatedly restarting industrial development initiatives. He said the government also needed to clarify which institution would be responsible for coordinating the policy, how progress would be monitored and what mechanisms would be used to secure private-sector participation. Okunsebor further said the country needed a framework for integrating its industrial policy with the wider African economic system. He proposed studying regional integration models, including those used by the European Union, while adapting them to Nigeria’s circumstances and the changing investment environment in Africa. He said any proposed regional integration council should be sufficiently flexible to respond to emerging investment opportunities and changing business practices. The working group also identified transportation and logistics, the cost of finance and human capital as critical areas requiring intervention to strengthen industrial competitiveness. Sola Magaji, Director of Impact Investment at NEEMA Capital, who represented the second working group, said Nigeria needed to distinguish between network infrastructure and infrastructure serving individual industrial facilities. “Network infrastructure includes roads, bridges and transport connections linking production centres to domestic markets, ports and export destinations. Facility-level infrastructure, by contrast, includes assets that can be developed within industrial clusters or by individual businesses”, she stated. Magaji said governments should take the lead in developing major transport networks and export infrastructure, potentially through public-private partnerships and other financing arrangements. Private-sector operators, industrial associations, cooperatives and businesses could then play a greater role in providing infrastructure within industrial clusters. She said access to affordable finance also remained essential to industrial expansion, urging policymakers to sustain efforts to bring inflation down and improve the operating environment for businesses. On human capital, Magaji argued that the cost of employing workers extended beyond wages and recruitment to include productivity losses arising from mistakes, inadequate management capacity and skills mismatches. She said Nigeria needed to develop stronger talent pools and ensure that vocational and educational institutions provided the skills demanded by employers. While acknowledging existing collaboration between some universities and businesses, he said similar arrangements should be extended to other technical and vocational training institutions. Magaji said improving graduate employability would reduce the additional costs businesses incurred in training workers who lacked the practical skills required for production. She also called for an integrated industrial energy system that would provide reliable and affordable electricity to industrial clusters. According to her, the government should develop a plan to power industrial centres using appropriate energy sources, including gas, solar, wind and hydropower, depending on the needs and circumstances of each cluster. She further advocated identifying and commercialising stranded electricity generation capacity by directing available power to locations where it could be used productively. Peter Akper, a member of the Steering Committee of the NESG Industrial Policy Commission, said the fourth working group focused on domestic value addition and export orientation. The group examined how Nigeria could strengthen linkages between manufacturing and the country’s agricultural, mining, petroleum and other natural resources, deepen local production capacity and enable Nigerian companies to compete under AfCFTA and in global markets. Akper said the group identified three priority value chains with the potential to generate wider economic benefits: mining and mineral processing, agro-industrial processing, and petrochemicals and gas development. He said developing these value chains would help Nigeria move beyond exporting raw materials towards processing more of its natural resources locally, creating industrial jobs and expanding the domestic supply of manufactured products. However, he said industrial competitiveness remained constrained by high energy costs, unreliable electricity supply, limited access to capital, inadequate logistics infrastructure, security concerns, standards compliance and regulatory bottlenecks. To address electricity challenges, the group recommended improvements to transmission and distribution infrastructure, alongside embedded power generation and mini-grid solutions for industrial users. It also called for stronger coordination between federal and state electricity regulators following the transfer of greater electricity regulatory responsibilities to states. Akper said better coordination would help prevent regulatory fragmentation from creating additional costs and uncertainty for businesses operating across state boundaries. On industrial financing, the group proposed blended-finance arrangements, stronger capitalisation of the Bank of Industry and measures to encourage greater deployment of pension funds into priority industrial sectors. It also recommended reviewing the cash reserve ratio applicable to banks as part of efforts to improve the availability of financing for productive investment. The group further called for increased investment in logistics infrastructure, wider use of existing infrastructure tax incentives and measures to attract private capital into transport networks. Akper said export performance was being held back by poor road and rail infrastructure, inefficient ports and limitations affecting the navigability of inland waterways. He also identified weaknesses in product standards and certification as barriers preventing some Nigerian goods from meeting the requirements of international markets. According to him, the multiplicity of agencies operating at ports also contributes to delays in processing exports, increasing costs for businesses and undermining delivery schedules. He said streamlining port operations, improving infrastructure and strengthening standards compliance would help Nigerian companies become more competitive in regional and international markets. Gabriel Aduda of the World Energy Council Nigeria, who represented the first working group, said Nigeria should transform its petroleum industry into a platform for broader industrial development rather than relying predominantly on crude oil exports. He said the group recommended five strategic priorities covering petroleum governance, local content, technology development, the transfer of industrial capabilities to other sectors, and coordinated investment. Aduda said implementation of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) and the local content framework needed to be strengthened through measurable targets covering regulatory coordination, investment certainty, production efficiency, transparency, environmental compliance and domestic value creation. He also called for clearer institutional responsibilities among petroleum-sector operators and regulators, arguing that uncertainty over decision-making and regulatory actions could undermine investor confidence. Aduda said Nigeria’s local content policy should move beyond measuring local participation and expenditure to promoting domestic manufacturing, engineering innovation, technology transfer and the development of intellectual property owned by Nigerian businesses. He cited the example of a company in Port Harcourt producing specialised high-pressure nuts and bolts for the oil and gas industry, arguing that businesses capable of manufacturing technically demanding components should receive the financing, certifications, research support and procurement opportunities required to expand. He urged oil companies to prioritise qualified Nigerian suppliers where they could provide the required goods and services, rather than automatically sourcing them from overseas. Such an approach, he said, would deepen domestic supply chains, create skilled employment and enable Nigerian manufacturers to develop the capabilities required to compete internationally. The group also proposed the development of interconnected industrial hubs focused on advanced engineering, equipment manufacturing, petrochemicals, industrial automation, digital technologies, materials testing and applied research. Aduda said technical expertise developed in the petroleum industry could also be transferred to mining, maritime services, renewable energy manufacturing, construction materials and healthcare equipment. He argued that these cross-sectoral applications would allow Nigeria to maximise the value of investments in technical training and industrial research. While acknowledging the need to address emissions, Aduda maintained that petroleum resources would continue to play an important role in industrial production, including the manufacture of chemicals, fertilisers, plastics and cosmetics. He called for increased investment in research and development to improve resource utilisation and reduce emissions while strengthening the domestic industrial base. Aduda also warned that Nigeria needed a deliberate succession strategy to develop the next generation of skilled oil and gas professionals as experienced workers and personnel from international oil companies were replaced. He said technical education should be linked more directly to identifiable industry requirements so that graduates could move into productive employment without extensive additional training. The group said the proposed reforms could strengthen petroleum governance, improve the competitiveness of Nigerian suppliers, attract productive investment and reduce the economy’s excessive dependence on unprocessed crude oil exports. Feese said the recommendations emerged from a series of consultations conducted by the NESG, including previous discussions on mining, the blue economy, power and oil and gas, as well as an industrialisation and competitiveness forum held earlier in the year. She said feedback from those engagements had informed the work of the Industrial Policy Commission and the design of the latest summit session. Read also: How states are deploying increased FAAC revenues to drive development The next step, she said, was to translate the recommendations into practical actions capable of producing measurable changes in Nigeria’s industrial sector. She stressed that industrialisation required a sustained national vision, supported by coordinated policies, private-sector investment and institutions capable of ensuring continuity across administrations. Feese said manufacturing-led industrialisation could also contribute to broader development objectives, including poverty reduction, innovation and productive employment. She urged businesses, professionals and other stakeholders to participate in the NESG’s Industrial Policy Commission beyond the annual summit, saying sustained collaboration was necessary to turn recommendations into implementation.
